title: Science and Technology
objectives: Làm summary completion có và không có danh sách từ, cùng diagram labelling
Đánh giá tuyên bố về công nghệ: thiết kế thí nghiệm, tái lập, kiểm định độc lập
Viết Task 2 dạng hai câu hỏi (two-part question) trả lời đủ và cân đối cả hai phần
Dùng cấu trúc phi ngôi và câu chẻ (it is … that, what … is) để nhấn mạnh trong văn học thuật
exam_strategy: Summary completion có danh sách: đáp án phải đúng nghĩa VÀ đúng ngữ pháp; danh sách thường có từ đồng nghĩa gây nhiễu. Không có danh sách: chép từ trong bài, kiểm tra số từ.
core_outcome: Đánh giá bằng chứng cho công nghệ mới (hiệu năng thử nghiệm khác hiệu quả thực tế); trả lời đủ hai phần của đề Task 2.

grammar.title: Impersonal structures and cleft sentences
grammar.explanation_vi: Văn khoa học dùng cấu trúc phi ngôi để khách quan: It has been shown that…, It is often assumed that…, There is evidence that… Câu chẻ giúp nhấn mạnh một thành phần: It is the data, not the algorithm, that causes most errors. / What matters most is independent testing. Hai cấu trúc này rất hiệu quả trong Task 2 khi muốn nhấn trọng tâm lập luận.
grammar.form: It has been shown / suggested that … · There is (little / growing) evidence that … · It is + X + that/who + … (câu chẻ) · What + S + V + is/was + … (câu chẻ với what)
examples: It has been shown that many systems perform worse outside the laboratory.
It is the quality of the training data that largely determines accuracy.
What researchers need most is access to independent test data.
examples_vi: Người ta đã chứng minh rằng nhiều hệ thống hoạt động kém hơn khi ra khỏi phòng thí nghiệm.
Chính chất lượng dữ liệu huấn luyện mới là yếu tố quyết định phần lớn độ chính xác.
Điều các nhà nghiên cứu cần nhất là được tiếp cận dữ liệu kiểm thử độc lập.
grammar.trap: Câu chẻ với what dùng động từ số ít is khi phần nhấn là một ý (What we need is more tests). Không lặp chủ ngữ trong câu chẻ (sai: “It is the data that it causes errors”).
items: It ___ been shown that the drug reduces symptoms. (has / is)
has
It has been shown that… = người ta đã chứng minh.
There is growing ___ that screen use affects sleep. (evidence / evidences)
evidence
evidence là danh từ không đếm được.
It is the battery, not the screen, ___ fails most often. (that / what)
that
Câu chẻ It is X that…
___ surprised the researchers was the speed of the change. (What / That)
What
Câu chẻ với What đứng đầu.
What the team needs ___ more independent data. (is / are)
is
Câu chẻ with what → is.
It is often ___ that new technology always saves time. (assume / assumed)
assumed
It is often assumed that = người ta thường cho rằng.
Rewrite as a cleft sentence: Independent testing matters most. → What ___ most is independent testing.
matters
What + V + is + X.
Correct the error: It is the data that it causes most errors.
It is the data that causes most errors.
Không lặp chủ ngữ it trong mệnh đề that.

readings.title: When a promising technology meets the real world
readings.strategy: Summary có danh sách từ: đọc bản tóm tắt, đoán loại từ, rồi chọn từ trong danh sách khớp nghĩa với đoạn tương ứng. Diagram labelling: tìm đoạn mô tả quy trình kiểm định và đi theo thứ tự.
readings.instruction_vi: Bài đọc khoảng 850 từ, 13 câu: 5 câu summary completion có danh sách từ, 4 câu summary completion không có danh sách (ONE WORD), 4 câu diagram labelling.
paragraphs: A

Every few months, a news story announces that a new technology can diagnose a disease, predict a flood or detect fraud more accurately than human experts. The claims are often based on genuine research, yet many of these systems never become widely used, and some that are introduced perform far worse than expected. Understanding why requires looking closely at the difference between performance in a laboratory and performance in the messy conditions of everyday life. The gap between the two is rarely mentioned in press releases, but it is often the single most important factor in deciding whether a technology will be adopted, and whether it will do more good than harm once it is.
B

Most new systems are first tested on a dataset collected by the researchers who developed them. A medical imaging tool, for example, might be trained and evaluated using thousands of scans from a single hospital. Under these conditions, model performance can be extremely impressive. The difficulty is that the scans may share features that have nothing to do with the disease – the type of scanner used, the way patients were positioned, or even small labels printed on the image – and the system may learn to rely on these clues rather than on the medical signs that matter.
C

When such a system is moved to a different hospital, with different equipment and patients, its accuracy can fall sharply. Researchers call this problem dataset shift: the data the system encounters in practice no longer resembles the data it was trained on. In one widely discussed case from the fictional Meridian Health network, a tool that identified a lung condition with ninety-four per cent accuracy in its home hospital achieved only seventy-one per cent at three other sites.
D

For this reason, scientists increasingly insist on external validation – testing a system on data from sources that played no part in its development. Ideally, this testing should be carried out by an independent team, since developers may unintentionally make choices that favour their own system. Some journals now refuse to publish claims of high accuracy unless they are supported by at least one external test.
E

Even external validation is not the final step. A system that performs well on historical data may still change how people behave once it is introduced. Doctors who trust a diagnostic tool may examine images less carefully themselves, a problem known as automation bias. If the tool makes an error, it may therefore go unnoticed. Several researchers argue that the true test of a technology is a prospective trial, in which its effect on real decisions and outcomes is measured over time, rather than its accuracy on a fixed set of past cases.
F

There are also questions of fairness. If a system has been trained mainly on data from one group of people, it may perform less well for others. Facial recognition systems, for instance, have been found in several studies to make more errors for some demographic groups than for others. Researchers describe such patterns as algorithmic bias, and they warn that bias can arise even when developers have no intention of discriminating, simply because some groups are underrepresented in the training data.
G

None of this means that new technologies are untrustworthy. Many systems have passed every stage of testing and are now used safely, from tools that check X-rays for broken bones to software that predicts demand on electricity networks. The lesson is rather that a single impressive figure tells us very little. What matters is where the figure came from, who produced it and whether it has been reproduced under different conditions. A modest result that has been confirmed several times is usually more valuable than a dramatic one that has been reported only once.
H

Responsible deployment therefore involves several stages. A system is first developed and tested internally, then validated externally, then introduced in a limited trial with close monitoring, and only afterwards used more widely. Even then, its performance should be audited regularly, since the conditions in which it operates can change over time. Each stage takes time and money, which is why commercial pressure sometimes encourages companies to skip steps.
I

For the public, the most useful habit may be a healthy scepticism towards headline claims. When a news report states that a machine outperforms experts, it is worth asking a few simple questions: was the system tested on new data, by whom, and has anyone checked whether it improves real outcomes? Such questions are not hostile to innovation; they are what allow genuinely useful innovations to be distinguished from those that only look impressive in a laboratory.

readings.title: Why replication matters
readings.strategy: Summary không có danh sách: bản tóm tắt theo thứ tự bài; đáp án là từ nguyên văn, kiểm tra số ít/số nhiều.
paragraphs: A

One of the basic principles of science is that a result should not be accepted simply because one team has reported it. Other researchers should be able to repeat the experiment and obtain similar findings. This process, known as replication, protects against errors, chance results and, occasionally, deliberate fraud. Yet for much of the twentieth century, replication studies were rarely carried out, because journals preferred to publish new discoveries rather than repetitions of old ones.
B

In the early 2010s, several large projects attempted to replicate well-known studies in psychology, medicine and economics. The results were sobering. In some fields, fewer than half of the original findings could be reproduced with the same strength, and some disappeared altogether. The finding that a particular study failed to replicate did not necessarily mean the original researchers had done anything wrong; small samples, chance and subtle differences in methods could all play a part.
C

Researchers identified several practices that made unreliable results more likely. Small sample sizes allowed chance effects to appear significant. Flexible analysis – trying many statistical tests and reporting only those that 'worked' – increased the risk of false positives. And the pressure to publish striking results encouraged researchers to present tentative findings as more certain than they were.
D

Since then, many fields have adopted reforms. One of the most important is pre-registration, in which researchers publicly record their hypotheses and planned analysis before collecting data. This makes it much harder to change the analysis after seeing the results. Some journals now accept papers on the basis of their design, before the results are known, so that studies with negative findings are published as readily as those with positive ones.
E

Data sharing has also become more common. When researchers make their data and code available, others can check their calculations and try alternative analyses. Critics note that sharing data raises privacy concerns, particularly in medical research, and that preparing data for others to use takes time that is rarely rewarded in academic careers.
F

The replication debate has not undermined science; if anything, it shows science correcting itself. A field that discovers and admits its weaknesses is more trustworthy than one that never examines them. For readers of science news, the practical lesson is to treat a single study, however striking, as the beginning of an inquiry rather than its conclusion.
G

Funding bodies have begun to support these changes as well. Several now set aside money specifically for replication studies, and some require researchers to explain in advance how they will share their data. Although such policies add work for researchers, supporters argue that they make public money for science far more likely to produce findings that last.

readings.title: How a smart irrigation system works
readings.strategy: Diagram labelling: đọc nhãn sơ đồ trước, rồi tìm đoạn mô tả từng bộ phận theo thứ tự dòng chảy của nước/dữ liệu.
paragraphs: A

Agriculture uses around seventy per cent of the fresh water taken from rivers and underground sources worldwide, and much of it is wasted. Traditional irrigation often follows a fixed schedule, watering fields whether or not the soil needs it. Smart irrigation systems aim to reduce this waste by giving crops only the water they require, when they require it. In dry regions, the savings can make the difference between a viable farm and an abandoned one.
B

A typical system begins with soil moisture sensors buried at several depths in the field. These measure how much water is available to plant roots and send their readings wirelessly every fifteen minutes to a central controller, usually a small computer housed in a weatherproof box at the edge of the field.
C

The controller combines these readings with a local weather forecast, which it downloads several times a day. If rain is expected within the next twelve hours, it may postpone irrigation even if the soil is fairly dry. When watering is needed, the controller opens electrically operated valves on the pipes leading to each section of the field.
D

Water is then delivered through drip lines, narrow tubes laid along each row of crops with small openings close to the base of every plant. Because water is released slowly and directly to the roots, very little is lost through evaporation or runoff. A flow meter on the main pipe records how much water each section receives, allowing farmers to check that the system is working as intended.
E

Trials on fictional farms in the dry Corran valley found that smart systems reduced water use by between twenty and forty per cent compared with scheduled irrigation, without reducing yields. However, the systems require reliable electricity and internet connections, and sensors must be checked regularly, since a single faulty sensor can cause a section to be over- or under-watered.
F

The cost of installation remains the main barrier for small farmers. Some governments now offer grants that cover part of the cost, and several cooperatives share a single controller between neighbouring farms. Researchers suggest that, as sensor prices fall, smart irrigation may become standard practice in regions where water is scarce.
G

Some agricultural advisers caution that technology alone cannot solve water shortages. Where rivers are overused, the water saved on one farm may simply be used to irrigate a larger area, leaving total consumption unchanged. For smart irrigation to protect water supplies, they argue, it must be combined with limits on how much water each region can take, agreed between farmers, local authorities and environmental agencies.

listenings.title: Students discuss a technology report
listenings.strategy: Multiple choice trong thảo luận: phân biệt ý kiến ban đầu của một người với điều cả hai thống nhất cuối cùng.
listenings.pre_listening: Trước khi nghe: gạch dưới từ khóa của câu hỏi (why, main, agree).
listenings.trap: Một sinh viên đưa nhận định rồi người kia phản biện – đáp án thường là kết luận sau phản biện.
listenings.transcript:
Tutor: So, Leo and Mei, you've read the report on the AI marking system that was trialled in secondary schools. What did you think?
Leo: My first impression was that it was a big success. The system's marks agreed with teachers' marks ninety per cent of the time on short-answer questions.
Mei: But when you read the details, the agreement on longer essays was much lower – about sixty-five per cent. And essays are where marking takes teachers the most time.
Leo: That's true. I suppose the headline figure was a bit misleading.
Tutor: What else stood out?
Mei: The schools in the trial were all quite large and well-funded. The report admits that results might be different in smaller schools with less experienced staff.
Leo: And the students knew the system was being tested. Some of them said they wrote more carefully because of that, so the trial conditions weren't entirely normal.
Tutor: Did the report look at how teachers used the system?
Leo: Yes, and that was interesting. Some teachers checked every mark the system gave, which meant they didn't save much time. Others accepted the marks almost automatically.
Mei: Which worries me, because the system made more mistakes with essays written by students learning English as a second language.
Tutor: So what's your overall judgement?
Leo: I'd say it could be useful for short answers, but it isn't ready for essays.
Mei: I agree. And we think it should only be used to support teachers, not to give final marks, at least until it's been tested in a wider range of schools.
Tutor: Good. In your write-up, separate what the report shows from your own recommendations. And mention who funded the trial – it was the company that developed the system.
Mei: Oh, we missed that. That's important.

listenings.title: How a new phone app is tested
listenings.strategy: Flow-chart: các bước theo thứ tự lời nói; nghe từ chuyển bước (first, once that's done, after that, finally).
listenings.transcript:
Speaker: Good afternoon. I'm Dana Whitfield, head of quality at Brightline Apps, and I've been asked to explain how we test a new app before it reaches your phone. It's a longer process than most people imagine.
It all starts with what we call the specification. Before any code is written, the design team produces a document describing exactly what the app should do and how it should behave. Every test we carry out later is checked against this document.
Once development begins, programmers write automated tests alongside the code itself. These are small programs that check whether each individual function works correctly. Every time a programmer makes a change, several thousand of these tests run automatically, usually within about ten minutes.
The third stage is what we call integration testing. Here we check that the different parts of the app work together properly – for example, that the payment screen correctly communicates with the bank. Problems often appear at this stage even when every individual part works on its own.
After that comes device testing. Our laboratory contains more than three hundred different phones and tablets, from the latest models to devices that are five or six years old, because many users don't replace their phones often. An app that runs smoothly on a new phone may be painfully slow on an older one.
Next is accessibility testing. We check that the app can be used by people with visual impairments, for example with screen-reading software, and by people who have difficulty with fine hand movements.
Finally, before a full launch, we release the app to a small group of real users – usually about two per cent of our customers – in what's called a staged rollout. We monitor crash reports and reviews closely, and only if everything looks stable do we release it to everyone.
The whole process typically takes between six and eight weeks for a new app.

questions.why: “what we call the specification”.

questions.why: “programmers write automated tests”.

questions.why: “usually within about ten minutes”.

questions.why: “Next is accessibility testing.”

questions.prompt: Stage 6: release to about ______ of customers
questions.why: “usually about two per cent of our customers”.

questions.prompt: This final release stage is called a staged ______
questions.why: “in what's called a staged rollout”.

questions.prompt: Total time for a new app: six to ______ weeks
questions.why: “between six and eight weeks”.

listenings.title: Lecture: the history of a simple invention
listenings.strategy: Bài giảng lịch sử công nghệ: theo dõi mốc thời gian và các yếu tố giúp phát minh được chấp nhận.
listenings.transcript:
Lecturer: Today I want to use one example – the humble refrigerator – to explore a broader question: why do some technologies spread quickly, while others take decades to be adopted?
The basic principle of mechanical refrigeration was understood in the mid-eighteenth century, and working machines existed by the eighteen-fifties. Yet household refrigerators did not become common in wealthy countries until the nineteen-thirties and nineteen-forties, almost a century later. So what took so long?
The first factor was infrastructure. A household refrigerator needs a reliable electricity supply, and until the early twentieth century, most homes simply weren't connected to an electrical grid. This is a common pattern: a technology often depends on a supporting system that has to be built first.
The second factor was safety. Early refrigerators used gases that were toxic or flammable, and there were serious accidents when they leaked. The development of safer coolant gases in the late nineteen-twenties made refrigerators acceptable in ordinary kitchens – although, as we now know, those gases later turned out to damage the ozone layer, which led to them being phased out from the nineteen-eighties onwards.
Third, price. The first household models cost more than a car. Mass production, combined with the option of paying in instalments, brought prices down to a level many families could afford.
The fourth factor is less obvious: changes in daily life. As more women entered paid work and fewer households employed servants, there was a growing need to store food for longer and shop less often. The refrigerator fitted these new patterns of living.
So the lesson is that adoption depends not only on whether a technology works, but on infrastructure, safety, cost and whether it fits the way people actually live. For next week, please apply these four factors to a technology of your choice.

questions.why: “by the eighteen-fifties”.

questions.prompt: Household fridges became common in the 1930s and ______
questions.why: “the nineteen-thirties and nineteen-forties”.

questions.prompt: Factor 1: a reliable ______ supply
questions.why: “a reliable electricity supply”.

questions.why: “toxic or flammable”.

questions.prompt: Later, coolant gases were found to damage the ______ layer

questions.why: “cost more than a car”.

questions.prompt: Prices fell through mass production and paying in ______
questions.why: “the option of paying in instalments”.

questions.prompt: Factor 4: fewer households employed ______
questions.why: “fewer households employed servants”.

questions.prompt: A technology must fit the way people actually ______
questions.why: “whether it fits the way people actually live”.

writing.instruction_vi: Đề có hai câu hỏi: trả lời ĐỦ CẢ HAI, mỗi câu một thân bài, mở bài nêu ngắn gọn câu trả lời cho cả hai. Viết ít nhất 250 từ (mục tiêu 270–310).
writing.task: Artificial intelligence is increasingly being used to make decisions in areas such as healthcare, education and employment. Why is this happening? What problems might it cause, and how could they be addressed? Write at least 250 words.
writing.sample_answer:
Artificial intelligence is now used to help diagnose illnesses, mark examinations and select job applicants. This trend is driven mainly by the promise of speed and lower costs, but it also raises serious concerns about accuracy and fairness, which can be reduced through independent testing and human oversight.

The main reason organisations are adopting AI is efficiency. Systems can process thousands of applications or medical images in the time a person would take to review a handful, which is particularly attractive when staff are scarce and budgets are tight. In addition, AI systems are often presented as more objective than humans, since they do not become tired or allow personal feelings to influence their judgements. Advances in computing power and the availability of large amounts of data have made such systems far more capable than they were a decade ago.

However, these systems can cause significant problems. A tool that performs well in a laboratory may make many more errors when used with different populations or equipment. Moreover, if the data used to train a system reflects past discrimination, the system may reproduce it, for example by rejecting qualified candidates from certain groups. Because many systems are difficult to explain, people affected by their decisions may find it impossible to challenge them.

These risks can be reduced in several ways. Systems should be tested independently on new data before being introduced, and their performance should be monitored regularly once in use. It is also essential that important decisions remain under human control, with people able to review and overturn automated recommendations. Finally, organisations should be required to explain how their systems work and to publish evidence of their accuracy for different groups.

In conclusion, AI is spreading because it promises efficiency, but its use in high-stakes decisions must be accompanied by rigorous testing, transparency and meaningful human oversight.

essay.prompt: Some people think that schools should use artificial intelligence to assess students' work. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
planning_prompts: Mở bài: lập trường (đồng ý một phần – hỗ trợ, không thay thế giáo viên).
Thân bài 1: lợi ích (nhanh, nhất quán với câu hỏi ngắn, phản hồi tức thì).
Thân bài 2: hạn chế (bài luận, thiên lệch với người học ngôn ngữ thứ hai, thiếu giải thích).
Kết luận: điều kiện để sử dụng có trách nhiệm.
model_paragraphs: Advances in artificial intelligence have made it possible for software to mark students' work, and some argue that schools should adopt such systems widely. I partly agree: AI can be a useful assistant for certain tasks, but it should not replace teachers' judgement in assessing students.

There are clear benefits to using AI for some kinds of assessment. For short answers and multiple-choice questions, software can mark large numbers of responses quickly and consistently, freeing teachers to spend more time planning lessons and supporting individual students. It can also give instant feedback, allowing students to correct mistakes while the material is still fresh in their minds, rather than waiting days for marked work to be returned.

However, assessing more complex work is a different matter. Essays and creative projects require judgements about argument, originality and style that current systems handle much less reliably. Trials have shown that some systems are less accurate for students writing in a second language, which could disadvantage groups who already face challenges. Furthermore, if students know their work will be marked by software, they may learn to write for the machine, using expected keywords instead of developing genuine understanding.

For these reasons, AI marking should be used only where its accuracy has been independently tested, and teachers should review its results, particularly for high-stakes assessments. What matters most is that students are judged fairly, not that marking is fast.

In conclusion, I agree that schools can benefit from AI for routine marking and feedback, but I disagree that it should be used to assess students' work in general. Teachers must remain responsible for important judgements about students' learning.

speaking.part2: Describe a piece of technology that has changed the way you study or work. You should say what it is, when you started using it, how you use it, and explain how it has changed the way you study or work.

speaking.model_answer: I'd like to talk about a flashcard app that I've been using for about two years to study English vocabulary. I started using it in my first year at university, when a friend showed me how it works. Basically, you create digital cards with a word on one side and its meaning and an example sentence on the other, and the app shows them to you at increasing intervals, so you see difficult words more often and easy ones less often. I use it almost every day, usually for about fifteen minutes on the bus to class. What has changed most is how I think about studying. Before, I used to read through long word lists the night before a test, and I'd forget most of them a week later. With the app, I review a little every day, and I actually remember words months later. It's also made me more aware of my own progress, because the app shows statistics about how many words I've learned. If I'm honest, it's not perfect – sometimes I just tap through the cards without really thinking – but overall, it's the consistency that it encourages that has made the biggest difference. I think it's a good example of how a simple technology can be powerful if it's based on how memory actually works.

deep.grammar: Modal verbs biểu đạt các cấp độ chắc chắn: 'may improve' không mạnh bằng 'will improve'. 'It remains unclear whether...' chỉ dùng khi chứng cứ không đủ, không phải câu đệm cho mọi bài luận. Phân biệt statistical significance với practical significance: một thay đổi nhỏ có thể có ý nghĩa thống kê nhưng không đủ tác động trong thực tiễn.
deep.reading: Đọc nghiên cứu công nghệ nên tìm thiết kế thử nghiệm, nhóm so sánh và hạn chế khái quát hóa. Một mô hình dự báo trong trường thí điểm không chứng minh được hiệu quả tại tất cả trường học. Với sơ đồ flow-chart, xác định trước mỗi bước cần hành động hay điều kiện, rồi dò câu chứa quy trình trong bài.
deep.listening: Bài giảng công nghệ thường dùng lập luận: hypothesis -> method -> findings -> limitations. Những câu 'at first we assumed' hoặc 'however' có thể đảo chiều thông tin. Sơ đồ ghi chép theo cấu trúc giúp không bị cuốn theo các thuật ngữ kỹ thuật gây xao nhãng.
deep.writing: Writing Task 2 lợi ích và tác hại của AI: không liệt kê 5 ưu điểm ngắn. Hãy chọn hai cơ chế quan trọng, ví dụ AI cải thiện khả năng tiếp cận phản hồi nhưng có nguy cơ tạo thiên lệch nếu dữ liệu thiếu đại diện. Câu kết cần nêu điều kiện quản lý cần thiết, không khẳng định công nghệ tự động tốt hoặc xấu.
